operatingConstraint: The volunteer store will not obtain permits, phytosanitary/health/origin certificates, or special regulatory approvals. Routine postal/customs declarations and recipient arrival declarations are distinguished from obtaining certification. Mandatory separate agency registration or advance notice is stated explicitly rather than called a certificate.

scope: Sealed 100 g retail pouches of plain Japanese steamed/dried Camellia sinensis sencha, sent from Japan by post to individuals for their own consumption. No live plants, fresh leaves, seeds, herbal mixtures, dairy, extracts, resale, traveller-baggage or gift-only assumptions.
method: Destination agriculture/biosecurity legislation and NPPO/food-authority rules, supplemented by Japan MAFF’s commodity-specific postal guidance. Each enabled destination has its own finding, channel analysis and sources or a shared-rule reference. A generic plant-product law is not assumed to resolve manufactured tea unless its scope or commodity schedule does so. Older rules, conflicting sources and inaccessible current schedules are disclosed.

catalog.weightCalculation: Maximum 100 g pouches = floor((maximum listed gross grams - 80 g outer packaging) / 120 g packed pouch).

statusDefinitions.allowed: Official evidence supports this finished product and import channel without a plant permit or phytosanitary certificate. Packaging, declaration, food-quantity/value limits and inspection powers still apply where stated.
statusDefinitions.conditional: A supported personal import route has specific quantity, packaging, inspection, notification or geographic conditions. Resolve the listed conditions before dispatch.
statusDefinitions.permit_required: Published evidence establishes a permit, approval or documented clearance route. This is not permission already obtained. A possible processing exemption must be confirmed before omitting documents.
statusDefinitions.certificate_required: Published evidence requires a phytosanitary certificate for the applicable route. Any claimed processing exemption needs the specific confirmation identified in the record.
statusDefinitions.not_verified: The research identified a material gap in the finished-tea classification, postal applicability, current rule or required documents. Not a finding that tea is prohibited; do not treat this destination as cleared.
statusDefinitions.domestic: Japan-origin shipment within Japan; no international agricultural import question.

priorReview: This report supersedes the earlier same-date review. Its verdicts address agricultural admissibility of personal postal tea, rather than equating carrier availability or commercial organic documentation with that answer.

EU-TEA.text: The common EU plant-health regime exempts finished dried tea from phytosanitary certification. Swedish guidance expressly covers private orders; Finnish guidance confirms processed tea is outside plant import controls. This applies to the 27 EU destinations and Åland below. Fresh leaves, live plants and herbal mixtures need separate assessment. Overseas territories are assessed separately.

EU-PRIVATE-ORGANIC.text: Austrian Customs guidance VB-0240 section 2.4(b), explaining EU organic import rules, expressly excludes personal/private imports sent by post. A private recipient consuming the tea does not need a commercial organic certificate of inspection. Routine customs declarations remain necessary.

MAFF-POSTAL.text: Japan MAFF’s 21 April 2026 postal matrix has a specific manufactured-green-tea column. Q means phytosanitary certificate; P means destination import permit; ◎ means no phytosanitary certificate. Footnote 11 notes that some cases fall outside plant quarantine and then need neither document; it does not identify which cases qualify. Confirm applicability with the destination. This reference guidance does not waive other laws.

limitations: This audit checks agricultural rules and identified personal-food import paperwork. It does not certify compliance with every labelling, food-safety, organic-claim, tax or carrier rule, or guarantee customs release.
Where a published rule requires an authority classification or a current schedule could not be obtained, the record is unresolved rather than assumed allowed or prohibited.
No published numeric cap does not mean unlimited personal quantities. All cited personal-use concessions require genuine personal consumption.
Value, frequency and package-count limits must be checked separately from net weight. Shipment splitting is not a way to evade aggregate allowances.

destinations.rule: MAFF-POSTAL. Conservative no-document exclusion on an explicit reading of Federal Law No. (7) of 2025. Article 1 includes live or dead plants and their parts; agricultural consignment separately includes plants. These manufactured sencha leaves remain physical nonliving plant parts under that broad limb, and Article 5(2) requires an exporting-country-authenticated phytosanitary certificate for every imported agricultural consignment. No further commodity designation is needed for this certificate duty. The separate manufactured-product limb is pest-risk qualified, so a specific-over-general contextual interpretation could exclude adequately manufactured tea; this material counterargument is preserved in definitionReview. This is a moderate legal-scope inference, not a tea-specific UAE ruling or an assertion of proven pest risk.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: Article 5(2) applies to every imported agricultural consignment without a commercial-sale, business-registration, baggage or quantity limitation. Article 1 importer includes natural persons and consignees. Japan MAFF's 21 April 2026 postal matrix expressly includes manufactured green tea and lists UAE Q*11. The separate personal-food guidance includes unaccompanied shipments and personal-food registration is exempt; no independent food-registration barrier is asserted.

definitionReview.actualCategory: The product remains identifiable physical tea leaves after steaming, rolling, hot-air drying and finishing. Article1 expressly covers dead plants/parts; the Arabic original confirms that wording. This is a stronger textual dead-material inclusion than TC's plant-parts definition without a living qualification. It does not mean every chemically derived plant ingredient is necessarily a plant part.
definitionReview.affirmativeDuty: Article1 agricultural consignment includes plants, plant products, or other regulated materials. Article5(2) then imposes certification on every imported/transit agricultural consignment. The final qualification concerning other regulated materials does not textually convert the separately enumerated plants limb into a future-designated-only category. Article3 limits application to cases specified by the Law and its executive regulations; Article5 is itself such an operative case. Article1's reference to a single certificate where appropriate describes consignment documentation and does not cancel the express all-consignment duty.
definitionReview.strongestContrary: Article1 definitions apply unless context requires otherwise. The more specific manufactured-product limb regulates manufactured materials only when their nature/processing can introduce/spread pests. MAFF-described sencha manufacture plus ISPM32 Category1 tea is strong factual evidence of sufficient processing. Reading finished tea exclusively in that product limb avoids overlapping definitions and fits Article2 pest-prevention purpose and Article4(1)(i)/(o) standards-related duties. This is a plausible favorable reading, not dismissed simply because tea is unnamed. It nevertheless requires the independent explicit dead-plant-part limb to yield; no provision in the full Act states that allocation. The conservative proposal retains the express dead-parts wording rather than claiming technical pest risk proved.
definitionReview.designationCheck: Article4 gives regulatory powers and Article14 permits further prohibitions/restrictions. Those powers are not the source of the proposed certificate duty; Article5(2) already supplies it directly for the defined consignment. Do not infer duty from mere enabling powers or customs tax-table absence.
definitionReview.exceptions: Article5(5)(c) is an administrative power to cancel prescribed conditions based on risk within the listed Ministry measures; it does not state a self-executing manufactured-food exemption. Article27(2) preserves older regulations only so far as compatible. The saved JKI partial German translation of Decision248/2003 Article2 uses living plants, but cannot narrow the newer Act's express live/dead definition. Its Article15(5) personal exception concerns traveler permits and Article25 small-quantity certificate exception concerns carried fruit/cut flowers/bulbs/tubers; neither establishes an automatic Japan postal-tea waiver. That partial translation is supplementary, not proof of absence of every possible older rule.
definitionReview.japanGuidance: Fresh original MAFF PDF page1 is dated21April2026 and has UAE Q*11 in the manufactured-green-tea column. Q means export with phytosanitary certificate; *11 warns some items may fall outside quarantine with neither permit nor certificate. JETRO August2025 separately states processed dried tea/matcha may be exempt subject to UAE confirmation; it predates the new Act. These are qualified corroboration, not an unconditional national duty or waiver.
definitionReview.privateFood: Existing personal-food registration exemption and unaccompanied-personal-food guidance are preserved. Their quantity/category gaps are not used as an independent certificate barrier. No commercial food documentation list is imported into private-post scope.
definitionReview.confidence: Moderate legal-scope inference supporting conservative operational exclusion; not a definitive tea-specific administrative determination.
definitionReview.comparisonWithTC: Both laws have an independent broad plant-parts limb and an affirmative document duty, despite a separate manufactured-product risk limb. AE additionally says dead expressly. TC uses prior permit sections34–35; AE uses Article5(2) certificate. This supplies a substantive consistent distinction from BH/MV/KN/VC living-plant-plus-risk-manufacture regimes.

independentPeerReview.assessment: Independently read current AE law previously; no further operative condition identified that defeats Article1 dead-part / consignment plus Article5(2) certificate chain. Contextual overlap and MAFF/JETRO possible exemptions are material contrary evidence, not a recovered controlling domestic waiver. Agrees moderate expressly conservative certificate-required leaf-part inference is defensible if applied consistently; no general permit conclusion.

destinations.name: Afghanistan
destinations.rule: Agricultural classification of finished sencha remains unresolved. Independently, the enacted 2025 Food/Medicine Anti-Smuggling Law, Articles 22–23, prohibits food import without licence or official permission and expressly covers companies and persons. The no-special-document route is excluded by a conservative inference from that unqualified rule; this is not a blanket tea prohibition.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: Articles 22–23 contain no business, resale, minimum-quantity or mode-of-carriage limit; Article 4 includes unlicensed importers and Article 23 names official and unofficial routes. Applying those provisions to a personal purchased postal parcel is an explicit conservative legal-scope inference. Article 21(1)’s separate trade-licence plus Health-permit duty is expressly commercial and is not treated as universal.

destinations.remainingQuestion: No unresolved question prevents the conservative no-special-document exclusion under the independent unqualified 2025 food-permission provisions. A published personal-food exemption or authoritative narrower application of Articles 22–23 could change it. Agricultural classification of finished sencha and current applicability of older agricultural provisions remain unresolved; no agricultural approval/prohibition is inferred from the food law.

destinations.name: Antigua and Barbuda
destinations.rule: Supported by a combined domestic-category and commodity-classification inference for the stated manufactured plain tea. The PPU’s 27 August 2020 all-country commodity table applies permit/phytosanitary requirements to Categories 2–4. Its signed 17 June 2021 guidance and current website require documents for regulated plant commodities and describe processed items that still carry pests; the PPU expressly operates within IPPC standards. Current-linked ISPM 32 section 2 and Appendix 2 identify tea as a Category 1 example. This is a reasoned application of the domestic scheme, not a freestanding international exemption. A broad older leaflet requiring certificates for non-regulated items was recovered in an IPPC report dated 14 May 2014; the ministry copy uploaded in 2022 changes only its contact email. Newer signed/current guidance supplies the operative narrower scope. Separate enacted food laws reviewed do not impose a blanket private-tea origin certificate.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: Product-scope inference applies to a clean sealed 100 g manufactured Camellia tea packet bought for personal use and sent by post; it is not a traveler or gift allowance. Ordinary customs declaration and arrival inspection remain.
destinations.authority: Antigua and Barbuda Plant Protection Unit
researchAttempts: Reviewed PPU import guidance and the 27 August 2020 commodity-status table, including processed-food examples. No explicit heat-processed Camellia tea classification or small postal waiver found.

2026-09-30: Re-read the current official PPU page in the browser. It regulates any quantity only when the article is regulated; processing examples include crushed herbs, dehydrated fruit/vegetables and other pest-bearing preparations, but do not classify steamed manufactured Camellia tea. Public generic processing guidance is exhausted without that commodity determination.

2026-09-30: Downloaded and read the complete 10-page official commodity-status table dated 27 August 2020. The all-country row specifically addresses Categories 2–4 and requires permit plus phytosanitary certificate; no Camellia tea/Japan entry or Category 1 processing determination appears. Rechecked current PPU guidance and targeted cooking/steaming/sterilisation/Category 1 guidance. No published product determination found; did not infer either automatic exemption or a Japan-origin ban.

Read official Public Health Act Cap. 353, Part VI: section 49 defines food and importer broadly; section 57(1)(a) authorizes food-import regulations for food intended for sale; section 66(e) enforces applicable food-import regulations; section 67 permits sampling of imported consignments. These provisions do not themselves create a blanket origin/free-sale/health-certificate requirement for private tea imports.

Read official Importation Protection Act Cap. 211 sections 3–6: section 3 authorizes controls for imported articles intended for sale and contains a rebuttable sale presumption. The express origin-health-certificate duty in section 4 applies to secondhand clothing, not tea. The traveller personal-effects exception in section 6 likewise concerns clothing, so it was not used as a food exemption.

Searched official legislation, ministry health guidance, food-import requirements and free-sale certificate terms. The located Food Safety Act 2017 file is in the Bills collection and the ministry labels its 2020 text Food Safety Bill; neither was treated as an enacted private-import obligation. No separate enacted blanket food-certificate or import-approval rule was established. The existing plant-risk classification gap therefore remains unresolved.

30 September bounded legal-scope peer review: The operative public guidance consistently limits permits and certificates to regulated commodities. The complete table addresses Categories 2–4; it is not a complete list of exempt Category 1 goods. Its examples include crushed herbs, dehydrated fruit/vegetables, and even a steam/pressure-treated tamarind commodity. These demonstrate that either being processed or having a heat treatment in the name does not automatically prove exemption. No table entry or local processing definition settles steamed/dried Camellia tea. Japan omission cannot itself be treated as a ban outside the regulated scope.

Fresh official media-index recovery found the 17 June 2021 signed Plant Protection Importation Guidelines and the apparently newer /2022/06/ import-export guide. Recovered the same broad guide from an IPPC national report published/updated 14 May 2014. Comparing normalized full texts shows the only change is the contact email domain; the 2022 upload is not evidence of a newly issued broader rule. Older guide requires certificates even for non-regulated items, while newer signed guidance/current PPU website expressly say regulated plant commodities.

Recovered and read the complete enacted Plant Protection Act 18/2012 from the national repository and searchable FAO mirror. Section 2 defines manufactured plant products by pest risk; section 15(2) allows NPPO requirements for certain covered articles, and section 16(2) uses international standards/risk analysis. No unqualified statutory certificate duty for every food or non-regulated plant-origin item was found.

Current PPU page expressly states that the agency operates within ISPMs. Re-read the complete 27 August 2020 domestic status table: all-country permit/certificate controls address Categories 2–4. Current-linked ISPM 32 section 2 and Appendix 2 (printed page 32-18) now supply the missing commodity evidence by listing tea as a Category 1 example. The Appendix is reference-only, not itself prescriptive; support is a combined-source domestic-scope inference for manufactured sencha rather than a universal processing exemption.

Rechecked the current Ministry of Health Laws & Regulations index online: it still labels the Food Safety text as Food Safety Bill 2020. Re-read saved enacted Public Health Act sections 57/66 and Importation Protection Act sections 3–6: food-import regulation powers and sale scope do not themselves create an unqualified personal-tea foreign certificate duty; the express certificate provision concerns used clothing. No separate mandatory special food document was established for this private packet.

destinations.rule: Plant Protection Act 2023–2, assented 16 February 2023 and commenced 29 May 2024 by SI 2024/23, replaces the previously cited Cap.268 (2007). Section 2 limits manufactured plant products to products whose nature/processing may create pest risk and section 2(2) expressly requires interpretation in accordance with ISPM 5. Sections 14 and 18(4) require internationally harmonised, scientific/risk-based measures. The current-linked ISPM 32 Appendix 2 illustrates tea as Category 1; normative Category 1 guidance says processing has made the commodity incapable of carrying quarantine pests and no phytosanitary measures should be required for pests eliminated by that processing. A domestic wholesome-food certificate issued following inspection is not a certificate the volunteer exporter must procure.

destinations.rule: Conditional support by applying the domestic pest-capability definition to factory-steamed, rolled and dried plain sencha. Act 10/1986 section 2 restricts plant products only when capable of harbouring or transporting plant pests; its other botanical categories concern propagative material and raw/unprocessed fruits or vegetables. Saved Importations Regulations 8(g) and their printed Explanation recognize cooked/parboiled/otherwise processed pest-free products as unlikely to introduce injurious organisms. Current-linked ISPM 32 Appendix 2 identifies tea as Category 1, providing manufacturing evidence rather than an automatically incorporated foreign exemption. Taken together, these support treating uncontaminated industrial retail sencha in clean new packaging as outside restricted-article scope. Regulation 8 itself waives regulation 4 entry/inspection only, not Act 3–4 permits/certificates. provisions.finding: Plant means living plants/parts. Plant product means processed or natural plant-based product exposed to pest-introduction/distribution risk because of its nature or processing. The risk phrase qualifies the class; processed origin alone is insufficient.

Other regulated articles are pest-capable objects deemed to require quarantine measures. Wood packaging excludes paper products. Commodity and consignment definitions remain limited to plants, plant products and other regulated articles.

Post-harvest pests and prevention during processing/storage are recognized. These general surveillance/control provisions do not independently require an import permit for every clean manufactured food. They preserve action against actual postprocessing contamination.

Scientific/PRA basis, import permits and release authorization attach to the defined plant/plant-product/regulated-article classes. Article4(4) addresses the restricted list, rather than bringing all nonregulated manufactured products within the law. The awkward English4(2) calls its origin-related document an import permit; no silent relabelling as a phytosanitary certificate is needed for the excluded-class inference.

Wood packaging has independent treatment/logo conditions. The scenario should use clean factory retail packing and paper/cardboard/plastic outer packaging without wood, soil, straw or raw plant filler.

The authority must discharge IPPC obligations under national law; delegated measures must accord with this Proclamation and relevant international phytosanitary standards. This is operative standards context, not mere international membership, but neither clause creates automatic direct adoption of every illustrative ISPM category.

Inspectors may inspect defined goods, suspend suspect consignments, collect samples and act on regulated pests. Ordinary truthful customs declaration and arrival inspection remain. No independent all-food import duty appears here.
Repeals Decree56/1971; disapplies inconsistent laws/customary practices; expressly continues Regulation4/1992 until replacement; effective on Gazette publication7May2026.

Plants include plant products and borrow the1971definition. Article3 subjects infestation-liable goods to quarantine. Articles4/6 impose permits/phyto on ScheduleI goods. Item11 names Camellia sinensis without raw/dried/manufactured specification. It is not confined on its face to planting material; some other entries expressly exclude seeds and ScheduleIII includes consumption imports. Its research/transit waiver is not a personal exemption.
Original EAA scan visually verified: leaves and products in natural, dried or manufactured state were included without a risk qualification. That definition is materially broader than2026Article2(2).

interpretation.application: Actual industrial steaming, rolling and drying produces manufactured sencha; current-linked ISPM32 Appendix2 tea Category1 is commodity-specific technical evidence that pre-existing plant-pest risks are eliminated by processing. The appendix is illustrative/nonprescriptive and does not itself waive a domestic law. It supports applying the actual2026risk-qualified domestic definition to clean sealed tea.
interpretation.continuity: Read Articles25(2) and26 together: compatible1992requirements continue for regulated Camellia plants/products, while the former1971unqualified manufactured-product breadth cannot override the new higher-law risk definition. The saved1992Article3 already conditions quarantine on infestation liability. ScheduleI lists a species, not expressly processed or dried tea as a distinct regulated commodity. It therefore need not be treated as a contrary determination that every manufactured derivative poses risk.
interpretation.counterargument: The1992definition incorporates the old broad manufactured scope, and ScheduleI expressly names Camellia. Article26continuation is unqualified in its sentence. A contrary reading could preserve that whole species category temporarily. The proposed interpretation rejects that blanket breadth because it would nullify the new Article2risk limitation and Article25(2)inconsistency rule; the schedule still has ample compatible operation for live/raw/risk-capable Camellia. This legal-scope inference must remain plainly labelled.
interpretation.limits: ISPM32does not address storage pests or postprocessing contamination. Clean new packaging, absence of pests/raw plant additives and ordinary inspection are conditions. No personal-use quantitative exemption is asserted.

destinations.requiredDocument: Executive-organ food-import permit under Proclamation 1112/2019 Article 10(1), on the explicitly stated market-supply interpretation of Article 3. Older directive health/origin certificates are not claimed as a proven unavoidable private-parcel duty.

foodScopePeerReview.scope: Food law only. Paid Japanese volunteer-store shipment of one sealed 100 g sencha packet to an individual for own consumption. No agricultural re-review.
foodScopePeerReview.recommendation: A conservative not_supported decision is defensible as an explicit legal-scope inference under current Proclamation1112/2019 Articles3 and10(1). Do not describe Directive22/2014 Article20 alone as an unequivocal current private-parcel certificate duty.
foodScopePeerReview.confidence: Interpretive/moderate; the public-store supply character, rather than the recipient being a commercial reseller, is the material assumption.
operativeChain: Current Proclamation1112/2019 Article3 is framed by the product being intended for market placement or otherwise offered for public use. It does not expressly limit its import provisions to Ethiopian companies or require the recipient to intend resale.

Article10(1) imposes safety compliance and an executive-organ permit on food import. A product publicly offered for sale by a store and dispatched on purchase to an Ethiopian consumer is reasonably treated as market supply, even though the end consumer will drink it personally. This is the decisive legal inference; no local-market-resale condition was located in Articles3/10.

Directive22/2014 Articles3/4 describe food-trade companies; Article2(8), however, defines food importer as any person importing by land/sea/air. Article8(1) expressly recognises personal-consumption imports and exempts them only from the certificate of competence. The same exception list includes research, relief and diplomatic imports, with Articles24/25 expressly treating some of those nonordinary-trade categories elsewhere in the directive.

Article20(4)(a) competence,20(4)(b) health certificate, and20(4)(c) origin certificate are distinct. The personal-food exemption can safely remove(a); its wording does not grant a blanket exemption from(b)/(c). That is contrary evidence to an affirmative claim that private personal food is outside every food-import provision, rather than conclusive proof by itself that all private imports require(b)/(c).

Article70 of the2019 law repeals earlier Proclamation661/2009 for covered matters and disapplies inconsistent instruments. It does not expressly reproduce an all-personal-food exemption. Article73 preserves a health-professional ethics body and functions, not a food-import exemption. Do not invent a broader saving clause. Current USDA2025 FAIRS commercial documents are corroborative only and cannot establish private scope.
foodScopePeerReview.strongestContraryReading: Read Article3 as requiring intended future market placement inside Ethiopia by the recipient, and Directive4 as strictly confined to Ethiopian food-trade companies. On that reading the own-consumption importer is outside Article10 and20, with Article8(1) merely clarifying the business-competence point. This is a substantial contrary argument; the statute does not define market placement here or expressly address international direct-to-consumer post. It prevents describing the conclusion as a tea-specific or expressly private-postal ruling.
foodScopePeerReview.whyNotSupported: The private-company exclusion is not sufficiently clear to affirm a no-special-documents route: it relies on adding a recipient-resale limitation absent from current Article3, and it does not account cleanly for the directive's explicit personal-import competence-only exception. For the store's stated paid public sales, the ordinary current market-supply reading supports excluding the destination under the no-permits policy, with that inference disclosed.
foodScopePeerReview.whatWouldReverse: An operative general exemption excluding direct-to-consumer own-consumption food imports from Article10, or a current published EFDA interpretation that Article3 excludes such purchased personal postal consignments. No bespoke tea letter is inherently needed; a general personal-import rule would suffice.
notClaimed: No proof that a private recipient must obtain a commercial competence certificate.
No inference from missing web results, medical/supplement exemptions, traveller allowances, or unavailable EFDA API.
No automatic exemption merely because the sender is volunteer-run.
No use of Directive20 as independent unquestioned private scope.

destinations.name: Grenada
destinations.rule: Food and Drugs Act Cap.110 (Act 14/1986), section 33(2), requires imported food to conform to origin-country law and be accompanied by an authentic document certifying that conformity and lawful sale. Section 2 defines food and importer broadly. Applying this unqualified duty to a private sencha parcel is an explicit legal-scope inference, not a tea-specific ruling. The newer Food Safety Act 19/2015 section 4(2)(a) excludes food imported for private consumption, so its own section 46 notice/certificate route is not applied here. It contains no express repeal of Cap.110, and section 46(4) preserves duties under other relevant enactments. The 2015 Act’s commencement notice and authoritative treatment of the overlapping statutes were not independently verified. Separately, the manufactured-tea plant-product classification remains unresolved; regulation 8(i) only exempts processed pest-free products from specified entry/inspection rules.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: The Cap.110 certificate conclusion is inferred from an unqualified imported-food duty and broad importer definition, with no published automatic personal-post exception established. Article 2 defines plants broadly including leaves/other parts and products as plant-origin material retaining its botanical nature until consumption; Article 6 ties measures to scientific/international standards with risk-analysis alternatives; Article 25(b) requires quarantine formalities and permits ministerial exemptions. Unlike Bahrain/Maldives, this source does not provide a clear living-plants/risk-qualified manufactured-product boundary. No automatic ISPM 32 exemption is inferred from the measure-setting duties. The FAO copy is not claimed to be the freshly recovered ministry consolidated/amended text.

destinations.rule: Current Sub-Decree 370 (28 December 2023; effective 1 May 2024) sets the permit/certificate lists. Plain green leaf tea HS 09021010 / heading 0902 is absent from its annexes. Annex 5 additionally exempts noncommercial imports of customs value US$1,000 or less from Annex 3 exporter certificates. The 2025 Customs manual provides ordinary postal/e-commerce clearance for individuals; unrestricted goods arriving through Cambodia Post do not need prior GDCE approval. Prakas 263 C (16 September 2019), Article 3, expressly excludes personal-use food imports from its imported-food procedure; its annex also classifies processed tea as low-risk.

destinations.name: Kiribati
destinations.rule: Biosecurity Act 2011 section 2 unconditionally includes products manufactured wholly or partly from plants within plant products, and all plant products within regulated articles. Finished sencha therefore falls within statutory scope (application to this product is an inference). Sections 25–26 make permits/certificates conditional on the applicable import specification; section 27 requires an advance written specification application only where no specification already exists. Section 31 exemptions require advance written requests and apply to a single importation. Food Regulations 2014 section 56 separately exempts personal-consumption food up to 10 kg per person from food-law requirements, not the Biosecurity Act. Section 26(2)(c) limits specifications to reasonably necessary risk measures, while section 26(3) requires a risk assessment and regard to SPS/international standards but permits precaution. These are rules for making the operative specification, not a self-executing exemption for processed tea.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: The Act establishes postal holding areas, and MELAD names incoming mail. The requirements therefore cannot be dismissed because the recipient consumes the tea personally.
destinations.authority: Kiribati MELAD Biosecurity and Plant Health; Biosecurity Act 2011
destinations.remainingQuestion: Current section 26 specification/saved earlier instrument covering finished plant-origin foods, or the relevant complete register showing none exists and thus triggering section 27. ISPM 32 tea risk evidence is relevant to the Director’s section 26 assessment but does not remove the Act’s unconditional manufactured-product scope.

Searched the authority for tea and processed-food import specifications; no tea-specific determination found.

Read Food Regulations and Standards 2014 sections 56–57: personal-consumption exemption up to 10 kg per person and ordinary food identification/inspection provisions. Kept this separate from plant biosecurity.

Checked the agriculture ministry’s newer website and Kiribati’s FAO country submission, which allocates prepacked processed-food inspection to Health; neither publishes a legal tea-specific biosecurity waiver.
Continued exact tea/Camellia/import-specification searches; no published applicable specification or written exemption found.

30 September independent scope reread: Act PDF pp.17–18 confirms unqualified manufactured-product and regulated-article definitions; pp.41–46 confirms conditional permit/certificate provisions and the no-existing-specification trigger for advance application. Section 80, p.91, provides for an office-based public register, so unsuccessful online searches cannot prove absence of a specification. Rechecked MELAD service text and the national FAO submission allocating processed/prepackaged food to Health; neither supplies the missing tea specification or a biosecurity waiver.

30 September independent food-document review: reread Food Regulations and Standards 2014 sections 53–64 in the FAO-hosted enacted text. Section 56 expressly exempts personal-consumption imports up to 10 kg from food-legislation requirements; section 57 permits identity-document checks for personal food. Sections 58–59 assess accompanying sanitary/analysis certificates and section 64 provides an inspector-issued arrival release permit. These provisions do not establish an advance foreign certificate or special registration obligation for every 100 g personal parcel; ordinary identity/arrival clearance is distinct from special advance paperwork. The existing biosecurity-specification gap remains unresolved. Saved text as pacific-food-sources/ki-food 2014.*.

30 September bounded remaining-scope review: Biosecurity Act 2011 section 107(2)–(4) preserves compatible old subsidiary rules, treating relevant import-treatment provisions as section 26 specifications. The 1976 Plants Ordinance itself was repealed; its sections 6 and 14 depend on notices/permits and its two schedules are forms/export fees, not an applicable tea specification. The missing existing specification therefore may be a saved older instrument, not necessarily a new 2011 publication. No such operative tea notice was recovered.

30 September definition/ISPM review: read full Act sections 2, 9, 24–31, 80 and 107 against the verified ISPM 32 Category 1 tea example. Section 26(3)(b) requires regard to international standards; it does not replace the import-specification mechanism or exclude manufactured plant products from section 2. ISPM 32 does not itself establish whether the existing Kiribati specification permits this parcel without special paperwork. No new request to inaccessible agriculture routes was made. Retained unresolved without adding a hypothetical food-law blocker.

30 September additional primary review: Biosecurity Act 2011 section 2 unconditionally includes manufactured plant products among regulated articles. Section 26 determines whether particular goods require a permit or PC, not a blanket permit rule. Section 27 expressly requires advance written application if the type has no specification. Sections 26(8), 79 and 80 provide a public register and office/Island Council inspection routes; electronic keeping is permissive. Compatible earlier instruments may survive through section 107. Re-read the full enacted statute including the public-register mechanism and current ministry incoming-mail/permit service page. The saved trade-portal procedure 119/step 141 is a meat workflow, not a general plant-food import specification. No public general processing exemption or complete online register was established; no repeated failed source routes pursued.
destinations.permitFreeReason: Manufactured tea is within the Act’s unqualified plant-product/regulated-article definitions, but that alone does not establish a permit or certificate: sections 25–26 expressly condition those documents on commodity specifications. Failure to locate a specification online is not proof that none exists; section 80 makes the register available at the Director’s office and Island Council offices. Section 27 would require an unacceptable advance application only if there is no existing specification. Routine arrival clearance/inspection is not treated as a special-paperwork blocker. The published personal-food concession does not settle the missing biosecurity specification.

destinations.rule: Combined-source legal interpretation: Plant Law 17-004/AU Article 3 limits manufactured plant products to those capable of carrying the relevant pest risk. Article 4 directs undefined terms to the IPPC/ISPMs; Article 39 requires phytosanitary measures to rest on pest-risk analysis and/or comply with current ISPMs; Article 46 applies that same standard to certificates. Read with the current-linked ISPM 32 Category 1 tea illustration and the actual industrial steaming/rolling/drying, plain manufactured sencha is inferred outside the regulated product class that triggers Article 44 permits/certificates. This is an explicit processing/classification inference, not a tea-specific Comoros ruling. Food Law 17-005/AU includes personal food but Article 63 refers plant foods to phytosanitary regulation and the examined certificate provisions do not create a separate universal private-tea certificate.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: The manufacturing-based interpretation applies to the goods, including paid personal postal orders; it does not borrow a passenger allowance. Plant Law Article 59 expressly covers post when imported goods are regulated. Ordinary customs declaration, lawful entry, arrival inspection and food safety remain applicable. Food Law Article 6(I)(g) includes personal consumption.
destinations.authority: Comoros Ministry of Justice; enacted Plant Protection Law 17-004/AU and Food Law 17-005/AU; IPPC current-linked ISPM 32
researchAttempts: Compared the old 2006 law in FAOLEX with the newer 2017 law from the Ministry of Justice; read article 3 definition and articles 44,46,59; searched implementing tea conditions.

Read Food Law 17-005/AU article 6 personal-use scope and articles 57–73 certification provisions; did not extend animal-product certificates to plain tea. Checked customs restricted goods. Examined WTO-filed 2022 technical-control and special-authorization drafts: their instrument numbers/dates are blank, so they are not proof of enacted exemptions; the organic-product provision inspected was an export provision.

30 September independent food/conformity pass: The Ministry of Justice publishes adopted Law 21-013/AU of 29 June 2021 on foreign trade, promulgated by Decree 22-004/PR of 18 January 2022. Articles 16–19 require customs/technical controls but delegate product lists, methods and competent administrations to separate regulations. The 2024 Ministry-hosted consolidated Customs Code preserves food/plant restrictions in transit provisions; it does not supply the missing private-tea import certificate rule. Previously reviewed 2022 blank-number/date drafts were not promoted to enacted law. Official Ministry source-index text read for articles 16–19 and current Customs Code excerpt. Direct full trade-law page retrieval failed; no new full adopted implementing instrument was downloaded.

30 September fresh official-online recovery: Recovered full Health Code 2011 directly from Justice Ministry. Articles 41–46 cover food hygiene; Article 43 prior authorization is specific to food additives, while Article 46 delegates standards/protection measures. Plain sencha is not thereby shown to require the additive approval. These provisions do not establish a private postal food-certificate duty.

30 September common-definition review: downloaded and read the full official 2017 plant law, including Articles 3, 4, 39, 43–47 and 59. The operative domestic IPPC/ISPM interpretation and measure/certificate clauses, together with current-linked ISPM 32 explicitly illustrating tea as Category 1, now provide the missing classification bridge for industrially steamed/rolled/dried retail sencha. Read Food Law Articles 6, 63, 71–73 and 126–129; preserved personal-use scope and actual label duties without extending business or animal certificate requirements. Reconciled previously examined health/trade laws and unadopted drafts; no hypothetical implementing duty was demanded. This supersedes the earlier unresolved classification, not the historical research record.
destinations.permitFreeReason: Supported for the stated sealed 100 g plain Japanese industrially steamed, rolled and dried Camellia tea, by the combined national-law/ISPM 32 interpretation. No permit, phytosanitary certificate, independent food certificate, advance plant-agency notice or special registration is established for this nonregulated manufactured product. This does not apply to raw/dried-only herbs, seeds, fresh leaves, blends or contaminated packaging. Package information must satisfy Food Law Articles 126–129, including translation into at least one official language (French is a practical option), identity/composition, manufacturer, origin/processing location, durability/storage/use, lot and accurate quantity.
destinations.independentFoodConformityRule: Food Law 17-005/AU Article 6(I)(g) includes personal use, so private consumption is not a general food-law exemption. Article 63 subjects raw/processed plant foods to phytosanitary regulation; Articles 71–72 apply previously specified certificates and market/distribution conditions, while Article 73 checks certificates supplied by importing businesses. None creates an independent unqualified certificate duty for the private plain-tea buyer. Article 126 requires package identity/composition/manufacturer, origin/processing location, durability/storage/use and lot information; Articles 127–128 require truthful information and accurate quantity; Article 129 requires information in at least one official language. Health Code 2011 Article 43 approval concerns additives, not plain tea. Foreign Trade Law 21-013/AU Articles 16–19 delegate technical-control lists/methods; delegation alone is not a document duty. Blank-number/date 2022 WTO-filed drafts are not adopted regulations and cannot establish one.

30 September finished-tea definition review, superseding the earlier unresolved scope inference: The better reading excludes a completely permit-free route. Section 204(a) expressly requires an import permit for a plant or product. In its plant-quarantine context, product reasonably includes manufactured tea without needing a separate bespoke commodity ruling or exact equivalence to the defined term plant material. Section 010(qq) includes leaves without a living/raw limit and 010(ss) expressly includes manufactured plant-origin items. Unlike Guam, these definitions supply no general processing exclusion. Section 238 permits dried food entry subject to pest freedom; it does not waive the independently imposed permit. Section 201 exempts non-regulated articles, not every admissible food. The ISPM 32 tea example supports a low-risk factual classification but is not incorporated as an exemption from this affirmative local permit duty. Section 010(cc) allows an import permit to be written or oral. Section 108(a) requires both oral and written permits for its specified higher-control plant shipments and describes an application route; it does not prove that this 100 g pouch necessarily requires a written permit or an advance application. Nonetheless an oral permit remains an authorization under the separate permit duty, not an automatic synonym for customs declaration or inspection. Sections 104/116/204/501 distinguish declaration, permit compliance, inspection and release. No retrieved provision makes ordinary postal inspection automatically satisfy the permit. The proposed exclusion rests on the user refusing permits at all, not on inventing a mandatory foreign certificate or claiming every permit must be written. destinations.name: Maldives
destinations.rule: The Attorney General’s current consolidated Plant Protection Act 12/2011, section 36, defines plants as living plants/parts (including seeds) and distinguishes unchanged/unmanufactured plant material, including grain, from manufactured products whose manner of manufacture leaves a risk of introducing or spreading pests. Sections 19 and 22 require certificates and permits for those defined controlled goods. Section 20(b) ties phytosanitary measures to applicable international standards or technical justification. Applied to the specified factory-made sencha (steamed, repeatedly rolled/pressed with hot air, dried and finished), these domestic category boundaries support a no-special-phytosanitary-document conclusion: it is a manufactured food, not living or merely raw dried plant material, and ISPM 32 section 2 Category 1 / Appendix 2 expressly identifies tea as an example of manufacture that removes plant-pest risk. This is a reasoned application of Maldivian statutory scope, not a claim that ISPM membership itself creates a waiver. The December 2025 and March 2026 ministry instructions govern covered plants/products and do not expressly expand section 36 to all finished food. Separately, MFDA-FCD STAN 6-2021 Rev.1 November 2025 permits personal processed food up to 5 kg/5 litres with intact identifiable packaging; its special advance postal form is for breast-milk substitutes, not tea. Section 37 of the 2011 Act expressly repeals Plant Quarantine Regulation 2008, so its old packed-food language is not relied upon as current authority.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: General commodity-scope interpretation applies equally to postal imports. Act section 25(b) expressly names post and courier services when handling covered plants/products/regulated articles; it does not make an otherwise outside-scope finished food a controlled commodity. This conclusion does not borrow a passenger allowance. The separate current MFDA standard governs the recipient’s noncommercial food use, including small parcels.

destinations.rule: The 1976 Plant Phytosanitary (Import Restriction) Notice expressly extends vegetative material, seeds and fruit to dried, frozen and chilled goods, but excludes goods described as cooked, or pickled and imported in bottles or cans. The actual printed item 64 contains the awkward wording "and mentioned herein" and requires certificates; it must not be silently rewritten as "not mentioned". The tea entry names vegetative material and seeds, not finished retail sencha. For this steamed product, whether the cooking exception applies and how the container qualification operates remain unresolved. The 2025 WTO review confirms the 1974 rules as amended in 1976 remain the operative starting point. The official historical Cap 185 section 2 applies its broad definition of plant, including dead severed leaves, to rules made under it unless context otherwise requires. The 1976 exception is expressly for purposes of that Notice, issued under Rule 9; the full 1974 parent Rules were not recovered to establish their exceptions or its effect on an independent parent duty.

destinations.rule: Supported by a combined statutory and commodity-classification inference for sealed manufactured plain Camellia tea. Plantenbeschermingswet 2020 article 1(1)(bb) includes manufactured products only when their nature/processing creates pest risk, and article 1(2) expressly gives IPPC/SPS term meanings and associated standards/guidelines priority. Current-linked ISPM 32 section 2 treats Category 1 commodities as requiring no phytosanitary measures; Appendix 2 expressly illustrates tea in Category 1. The Appendix is reference-only, not a freestanding binding exemption, but supplies the missing commodity evidence when applying the domestic definition. Articles 5–8/14 and the August 2026 notice control covered plants/products; neither specifically reclassifies manufactured tea. The separate trade Negative List omits tea and no enacted private-food certificate requirement was established.

destinations.rule: Conservative no-document exclusion by explicit domestic legal-scope inference. Section 34(2)(a) requires prior permits for all regulated articles, not just a subsequently designated list; section 39(2) and 2024 regulations 25–27 expressly include mail/courier. Packaging is also named separately, but hypothetical pouch capability is not the basis of this exclusion. Domestic ISPM-congruence duties and the Category 1 manufacturing reading are the strongest contrary interpretation, preserved in definitionReview. No automatic provision recovered reconciles them by expressly excluding these nonliving leaves. Private-food controls supply no separate certificate barrier.

The 2024 fee schedule expressly distinguishes home-consumption permits.

foodArrivalPeerReview.scope: Paid 100 g factory-sealed Japanese plain industrially steamed, rolled and dried Camellia tea for personal drinking. No separately obtained permits, certificates, agency registration or advance notice; ordinary customs and arrival inspection/fees allowed.
foodArrivalPeerReview.conclusion: A defensible lawful route exists through destination inspection under regulation7, applied for by ordinary accurate customs declaration under regulation8(1) upon arrival. No independent preobtained CoC, exemption letter or digital conformity mark is established for tea on that route. Mandatory standards compliance, possible testing/fees and the authority-issued import clearance certificate remain. This is a combined-provision legal interpretation, not an assurance of immediate or cost-free postal release.

routeAnalysis.finding: Schedule 1 Part 1 Group X includes food and food products. Regulation 6 expressly applies assessment whether goods are for trade or personal use. No invented personal-food exemption is needed.

Regulations 5(2), 5(5)(a) and Schedule 1 Part 2 item 1 exempt consignments with FOB value at most USD 2,000 (except used vehicles) from pre-export verification. Regulation 8(2)(i) can require an exemption letter where applicable to a regulation 5(5) route. However, regulation 7(1) expressly operates notwithstanding regulation 5 and directs destination inspection for Part 1 goods lacking a CoC. It does not restrict that alternative to higher-value goods or exclude goods also satisfying Part 2. Food remains Group X even when low-value. Regulation 10(1)(a) repeats the no-CoC destination route. Entry need not rest on a letter-dependent exemption.

routeAnalysis.issue: Does automatic low-value status compel a letter regardless of route?
routeAnalysis.finding: Strongest contrary reading: regulation 5(5)(a) says the goods shall be exempt, and 8(2)(i) points to 5(5), so low-value goods might routinely be channelled into exemption-letter verification. Preferred reading: the automatic exemption removes origin verification; it neither prohibits destination inspection nor imposes an unconditional letter duty. Regulation 7 expressly overrides regulation 5, while 8 requires a letter only where applicable. A universal letter prerequisite would obstruct regulation 7 despite its unqualified no-CoC trigger. This does not mean every low-value exemption procedure is letter-free, or guarantee whether a surcharge will be imposed.

Regulation 8(1) defines the application as an accurate customs declaration through the electronic single window, before or upon arrival. Regulation 8(2)(a–e) lists normal transport, packing, invoice, customs and transit records; the foreign CoC in (f) and exemption letter in (i) are conditional. Japanese plain tea does not fall within the EAC product-permit, vehicle export-certificate, returning-resident passport or diplomatic-note categories. Regulations 7(3) and 10(6) direct the inspector to issue the ICC after conformity is established; regulation 12 requires it before release. This ICC is the output of arrival inspection, not a special document the Japan store must obtain beforehand.

SI 112/2022 regulation 13(3) requires pre-clearance evidence of digital marks only for Certification Regulations 2021 Schedule 3 Part II categories. The complete schedule lists cosmetics, electricals and construction materials, not tea or food. Full SI 108/2022 section 13 only changes the fee from 18 to 21 shillings per unit. Section 2 retains the Part II cross-reference; section 11 inserts regulation 23A(1), a conformity duty, and 23A(2), a marking duty for locally manufactured Part II goods. The amendment does not extend digital marks to tea. Manufacturing certification under 2021 regulation 4 is not a general private-import permit.

The official 8 September 2026 UNBS news says importers can create an account with a TIN and email, describes Customs integration and automatic ICC generation, and confirms destination inspection without PVoC, with a 15% CIF surcharge. It does not say every private postal recipient must independently register. Statutory regulation 8(1) affirmatively accepts a customs declaration upon arrival. An account interface does not displace that route without a universal registration duty. Do not claim a paper CN22 alone necessarily supplies every required customs data field.

Schedule 1 Part 3 item 1 excludes food from the low-value destination-inspection exemption, so tea remains inspectable and testable. Regulation 7(2) provides a 15% CIF surcharge and applicable inspection or other fees. Schedule 2 paragraph 2 sets a destination fee of 0.5% CIF (minimum USD 235, maximum USD 3,000), but expressly disapplies that fee below USD 1,300 CIF. Laboratory charges under paragraph 3, incidental storage and ordinary customs costs can remain. No exact fee total is promised.

conditions: Preserve the accepted agricultural conditions: finished plain manufactured tea, clean new appropriate packaging, no raw plant material or pests.
Provide an accurate normal postal/customs declaration and invoice, packing and transport details; transmit the declaration through the single window as prescribed.
Allow arrival conformity inspection/testing, meet food standards, shelf-life and label rules, and pay applicable charges.
Do not rely on a pre-export CoC, special exemption letter or digital mark. Do not advertise inspection-free entry.

destinations.name: Saint Vincent
destinations.rule: Plant Protection Act 16 of 2005 section 2 limits plants to living material and manufactured plant products to products whose nature or processing may create pest-introduction/spread risk. Sections 10(2) and 11 attach permits/certificates to specified covered articles rather than all plant-derived food. The manufactured-tea facts and ISPM 32 Category 1 example supply a reasoned factual basis for applying the statutory boundary without a bespoke tea ruling. The regulated-article definition concerns material capable of carrying/spreading pests and deemed to require measures; clean new retail/postal packaging alone is not evidence of such a designation. The 2019 ministry notice applies to covered plant parts/products and is not read to erase section 2. The newly recovered official two-page commodity guidance names planting materials and specific fruits, roots, flowers and vegetables, not tea; it is undated and not treated as an exhaustive current waiver. Section 15 postal reporting and section 12 inspection remain ordinary controls and do not expand the defined commodity class.
destinations.personalMailApplicability: This conclusion follows commodity scope in the applicable local law, not a baggage, gift or noncommercial-seller exception. It applies to the stated private direct postal purchase and clean new packaging.
